problem: End-to-end VLM planners are black boxes that hallucinate numerical actions, VLM-as-trajectory-selector methods are limited by sampling quality and diversity, and VLM costmap methods need detailed human instructions and so are not autonomous.
motivation: Social navigation needs the semantic reasoning of VLMs, but a robot deployed in the real world needs reliability, interpretability and safety. The costmap is a mathematically sound interface between VLM reasoning and classical planners. Noisy tracking and VLM latency also break naive deployments.
key_idea: Use the VLM not to plan but to output traversable regions and social scores for tracked agents, which are grounded into a BEV costmap that is checked by VLM upstream verification and a high-frequency LiDAR reflex-zone safeguard.
insight: Traversability identification and social scoring matter most: on SCAND, removing scoring raises L2 from 0.55 to 1.12 and removing traversability raises it to 0.84, while removing verification costs little (0.57). Removing the safeguard does not hurt the offline metric (L2 0.48) because the human operator never had to make urgent avoidances. The safeguard matters in autonomous operation, as the qualitative examples show. Asynchronous costmap updates beat path-etiquette's lower-frequency trajectory selection with the same VLM.
method: Open-set perception: RAM++ tags, GroundingDINO boxes, depth registration by projecting boxes into the LiDAR cloud and DBSCAN clustering, and Kalman-filter tracking of each object's state (box, position, velocity).
Traversability identification: the VLM picks the traversable ground region and lists non-traversable ones at every step; SAM produces a binary traversable mask M.

Social scoring: the VLM drops irrelevant objects and gives the rest a bounded score, higher for immediate danger. Humans moving in the robot's direction (social leaders) get a negative score. New objects get a default score until the VLM analyses them, which keeps the pipeline asynchronous.

Upstream verification: the VLM checks whether each object's depth and heading match the images. A depth mismatch triggers re-registration that excludes the false cluster. A heading mismatch raises the object's social score.
Costmap: C = λ1 C_goal + λ2 C_obs + λ3 C_obj + C_trav, where C_obj is a sum of elliptical Gaussians weighted by social score and shaped by velocity, and C_trav penalises cells outside M.
Reflex safeguard: a dynamic zone (box or arc, T=1.5 s, W=0.8 m) along the predicted trajectory. LiDAR points in it that belong to no tracked object add high costs to the costmap.
Local controller: gradient descent on the costmap generates the trajectory and Pure Pursuit tracks it.

setting.backbone: Qwen3.5-2B (frozen, offline SCAND); GPT5.4-Nano (frozen, real robot); plus RAM++, GroundingDINO, SAM
setting.training_data: none (training-free; costmap weights tuned by grid search on the longest SCAND trial)
setting.observation: monocular RGB image history + LiDAR point cloud (Livox Mid-360) + odometry
setting.action_space: trajectory waypoints tracked by Pure Pursuit
setting.simulator: real world only (SCAND recorded dataset plus real deployment)

numbers_note: Custom real-world and SCAND evaluations only; no standard navigation benchmark is used.
results: On SCAND, G2-Nav reaches L2 0.55 m and MAOE 15.64°, the best MAOE, ahead of CityWalker (0.60 / 16.81) and path-etiquette (0.97 / 20.14). In the real campus deployment it has the lowest average time (278 s vs PAP 322 s) and the second-best safety violation time (6.9 s) and distance (172.3 m). Social Force is the only method better on those two, at 4.4 s and 165.4 m.
limitations: Latency on edge devices (about 4 s VLM query) and a heavy multi-step perception pipeline.
The safeguard only checks unregistered nearby LiDAR points, gives no formal safety guarantee and does not avoid local minima.
Small real-world evaluation (6 trials per method, one environment); the offline SCAND metrics do not test closed-loop safety.
